Abroad
ä-brôd'
adv. (widely, out of doors, in foreign parts; rendering Hebrew puts in the causative, Greek ekchuno and diaphemizo)
A compound of a (on) and broad — at large, over a wide space. In Scripture it attaches to three verbs above all: scattering, spreading, and making known, and the same idea of dispersion serves for judgment and for mission.

Biblical Definition

Abroad means at large or widely, and its biblical uses turn on dispersion. It records the spread of the nations from Babel onward: “afterward were the families of the Canaanites spread abroad” (Genesis 10:18). It carries the covenant threat of exile: “If ye transgress, I will scatter you abroad among the nations” (Nehemiah 1:8) — which Nehemiah quotes back to God in prayer, along with the promise attached to repentance. Ezekiel uses it of shepherds who scatter the flock they were given to feed: “ye have thrust with side and with shoulder, and pushed all the diseased with your horns, till ye have scattered them abroad” (Ezekiel 34:21). But the word is also the vehicle of the gospel's spread: the shepherds at Bethlehem “made known abroad the saying which was told them concerning this child” (Luke 2:17), and Paul writes that “the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost” (Romans 5:5). What judgment scatters, grace also spreads.

Webster 1828 Definition

At large; widely; out of doors or in foreign parts. In Scripture it attends the scattering of nations in judgment, the exile threatened for transgression, and equally the spreading abroad of the gospel and of the love of God in the heart.

expand to see more

ABROAD, adv. [a and broad.] At large; widely; over a wide space.

2. Out of the house; as, he is gone abroad.

3. In foreign countries; beyond the borders of one's own land.

4. Extensively; before the public; as, the report is spread abroad.

5. In Scripture, I will scatter you abroad among the nations, Neh. 1; the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts, Rom. 5.

Key Scripture

Genesis 10:18 — "And the Arvadite, and the Zemarite, and the Hamathite: and afterward were the families of the Canaanites spread abroad."

Nehemiah 1:8 — "Remember, I beseech thee, the word that thou commandedst thy servant Moses, saying, If ye transgress, I will scatter you abroad among the nations:"

Ezekiel 34:21 — "Because ye have thrust with side and with shoulder, and pushed all the diseased with your horns, till ye have scattered them abroad;"

Luke 2:17 — "And when they had seen it, they made known abroad the saying which was told them concerning this child."

Modern Corruption

Scattering appears in Scripture as a judgment, and yet God repeatedly turns it into the means of blessing — Babel into the nations, exile into the synagogues of the dispersion, and the persecution of Acts 8 into the first missionary expansion.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is that God overrules judgment for mission. The scattering from Babel was a sentence on human pride, and it produced the nations to which the gospel was afterward sent. The exile was the covenant curse executed, and it planted Jewish communities across the empire, which became the first synagogues Paul preached in. Acts 8 states the pattern most compactly: a great persecution arose, and they were all scattered abroad — and the next clause is that they that were scattered went everywhere preaching the word.

Ezekiel 34 keeps the doctrine from becoming a comfortable fatalism. The shepherds who scattered the flock are not excused because God brought good out of it; they are indicted, and the chapter ends with God declaring that He will Himself seek out His sheep and set one shepherd over them. Providence overruling a sin never lessens the sin. Joseph put both truths in one sentence to his brothers — ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good — and both halves have to be said.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew puts in the causative is to scatter or disperse; pazar is to scatter as seed. Greek diaspeiro gives diaspora, the dispersion, and ekchuno is to pour out, the verb of Romans 5:5.

expand to see more

Hebrew puts (H6327) — to scatter, disperse, break up; the verb of Babel and of the exile.

Hebrew pazar (H6340) — to scatter, as seed is scattered; used both of dispersion and of liberality.

Greek diaspeiro (G1289) — to scatter abroad; whence diaspora, the dispersion of Israel.

Greek ekchuno (G1632) — to pour out; the verb behind shed abroad in our hearts.

Greek diaphemizo (G1310) — to spread abroad a report; used of the news of Christ's miracles.

Usage

"Of the nations dispersed after Babel: afterward were the families of the Canaanites spread abroad (Genesis 10:18)."

"Of the exile threatened in the covenant: If ye transgress, I will scatter you abroad among the nations (Nehemiah 1:8)."

"Of the gospel and the love of God spread widely: made known abroad the saying which was told them (Luke 2:17)."
